evidence.claim: River roads circle a freight canal turned parkland in central New Jersey
evidence.quote: The land between Canal and River Roads is now part of the Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park.

evidence.claim: River Road winds beside the Millstone River; Canal Road follows the Delaware and Raritan Canal on the valley’s eastern side.
evidence.quote: To the west is River Road, winding alongside the Millstone River, and to the east Canal Road follows the banks of the Delaware and Raritan Canal.

evidence.claim: Together they form the Millstone Valley Scenic Byway loop through central New Jersey.
evidence.quote: The Millstone Valley National Scenic Byway is a loop formed by two roughly parallel roadways

evidence.claim: Its sponsor, the Millstone Valley Preservation Coalition, credits national and state designation to the valley’s scenery, historical importance and environmental integrity.
evidence.quote: The Millstone Valley Scenic Byway received national and state designation for its scenic beauty, historic importance, and environmental integrity.

evidence.claim: State designation came in 2001, followed by national recognition in 2009.
evidence.quote: It was designated a New Jersey Scenic Byway in 2001 and it became one of two New Jersey Scenic Byways that were nationally designated in 2009.

evidence.claim: The roads draw on an older network of trails that followed and crossed the river in the homeland of the Lenni Lenape.
evidence.quote: was home to the Lenni Lenape people before settlers arrived. The river served as an early means of transportation as did Indian trails, which both paralleled and crossed the river.

evidence.claim: Those trails became the area’s roads, including Canal Road and River Road.
evidence.quote: These trails later became the roadway system for this area, including Canal Road and River Road which comprise the core of the Byway.

evidence.claim: The canal later carried coal, farm products and manufactured goods toward New York for a century.
evidence.quote: Passing northward through the Millstone Valley, the Delaware & Raritan Canal played a vital role for a century, helping to deliver coal, agricultural products, and manufactured goods to the booming New York metropolis.

evidence.claim: Land between the two roads now belongs to Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park.
evidence.quote: The land between Canal and River Roads is now part of the Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park.

evidence.claim: Starting at Rocky Hill, the loop reaches Kingston before following the canal side north through Griggstown.
evidence.quote: It travels along CR 603 (Kingston-Rocky Hill Road) and Canal Road on the east side of the Delaware and Raritan Canal.

evidence.claim: At Griggstown, an original bridgetender’s house serves as the byway visitor center.
evidence.quote: The Visitor Center is in one of the original D&R Canal bridgetender’s houses

evidence.claim: Continue toward Millstone and East Millstone, linked near the loop’s northern end by County Route 514, then return along the river side.
evidence.quote: The route loops back on the south side at Route 27 in Princeton and Kingston and connects near the northern end via CR 514 between Millstone and East Millstone.

evidence.claim: north through Griggstown
evidence.quote: Beginning at the southern end of the Byway and leading north, they are: Kingston Mill District Kings Highway Historic District Kingston Village Historic District Delaware and Raritan Canal National Register District Rocky Hill Historic District Griggstown Historic District

evidence.claim: Rocky Hill’s old nickname, the Devil’s Featherbed, described ground that was difficult to cross by horse and wagon before road improvements.
evidence.quote: Before roads were improved, it was known as the Devil's Featherbed because it was difficult to travel the rocky terrain by horse and wagon.

evidence.claim: In 1783, George Washington stayed at Rockingham, the Berrien family’s house.
evidence.quote: In 1783, during the American Revolutionary War, General George Washington camped at Rockingham, the house owned by the Berrien family.

evidence.claim: The village’s major growth came later, in the second quarter of the nineteenth century, as a stop between Princeton and New Brunswick.
evidence.quote: its major growth period to the second quarter of the 19th century, as a stop between Princeton and New Brunswick.

evidence.claim: Its historic district includes the Dutch Reformed Church, built in 1856 in the Carpenter Gothic style.
evidence.quote: most notable of being the Dutch Reformed Church that was built in 1856 in the Carpenter Gothic style.

evidence.claim: Rockingham itself has been relocated; the byway listing places it in Kingston.
evidence.quote: the relocated Rockingham site in Kingston

evidence.claim: At Griggstown, the byway visitor center occupies an original canal bridgetender’s house.
evidence.quote: The Visitor Center is in one of the original D&R Canal bridgetender’s houses

evidence.claim: Inside, the kitchen is furnished to represent 1840–1860; the garden combines period medicinal plants with vegetables for the table.
evidence.quote: its kitchen is interpreted and furnished for the period 1840-1860; a lovely garden contains period medicinal plantings and favorite table vegetables.

evidence.claim: The settlement’s name reaches further back than the canal, to Benjamin Griggs and his gristmill on the Millstone River.
evidence.quote: Griggstown was named after Benjamin Griggs, who established a grist mill on the Millstone River

evidence.claim: That mill became a meeting place for European farmers and the center of the emerging community.
evidence.quote: served as a meeting place for the European farmers of the area and as such the center of the community that would become Griggstown.

evidence.claim: The river and canal both pass through the village.
evidence.quote: The Millstone River and the Delaware and Raritan Canal both flow through Griggstown.

evidence.claim: Millstone was once Somerset Courthouse, the county seat from 1738 until British forces burned it in 1779.
evidence.quote: Millstone, then called Somerset Courthouse, was the county seat of Somerset County from 1738 until the British burned it to the ground in 1779

evidence.claim: After the Battle of Princeton in January 1777, Washington spent a night at the Van Doren house while his army camped nearby.
evidence.quote: After the victory at Princeton on January 3, 1777, General George Washington headquartered at the Van Doren house, while the army camped nearby that night.

evidence.claim: They marched on to Pluckemin the next day, bound for winter quarters at Morristown.
evidence.quote: The next day, they marched to Pluckemin on the way to their winter encampment at Morristown.

evidence.claim: Another brief connection came with the Mercer and Somerset Railway in the 1870s: a bridge linked it across the river to the Pennsylvania Railroad’s line.
evidence.quote: Millstone was briefly connected to the Pennsylvania Railroad when the Mercer and Somerset Railway was extended to the town in the 1870s and connected via a bridge across the Millstone River to the Pennsylvania Railroad's Millstone and New Brunswick Railroad

evidence.claim: The arrangement ended before the 1880s, but remnants of the bridge remain visible.
evidence.quote: that arrangement did not last into the 1880s. Remnants of the railroad bridge can still be seen.

evidence.claim: The drive occupies the river’s long, narrow floodplain, and its roads pass through eleven historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: The long and narrow Millstone Valley is the flood plain of the Millstone River and its many tributaries.

evidence.claim: its roads pass through eleven historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: The Millstone Valley Scenic Byway passes through eleven distinct historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places

evidence.claim: In 1777, the Continental Army marched up this valley after its victory at Princeton.
evidence.quote: The Continental Army marched up the valley in 1777, following the victory at the Battle of Princeton.

evidence.claim: The district’s National Register listing recognizes its archaeology, architecture and commerce.
evidence.quote: The district was added to the National Register of Historic Places on July 8, 1982, for its significance in archeology, architecture and commerce.

evidence.claim: The historic district also includes a bridgetender’s station and a locktender’s house, both built for the canal.
evidence.quote: The Bridge Tender's House, the Bridge Tender’s Station and the Lock Tender's House, all built for the Delaware and Raritan Canal, are contributing buildings.

evidence.claim: The visitor-center garden includes medicinal plants and table vegetables selected to represent the canal era.
evidence.quote: a lovely garden contains period medicinal plantings and favorite table vegetables.

evidence.claim: River roads circle a freight canal turned parkland in central New Jersey
evidence.quote: The 27-mile Byway encircles a portion of the Millstone River in central New Jersey.

flags: Mileage unresolved: NJDOT says 25 miles in its introduction and approximately 27.5 in fast facts; the sponsor says 27. Omitted a single length.
NJDOT cache includes unrelated Route 29/Delaware River material; excluded it.
Sponsor page mixes 2026 visitor-center dates with older opening notices. No hours or opening promise included.
NJDOT uses Lenni Lenape; town pages use Lenape. Used NJDOT terminology for its historical account; no tribal-authored source is cached.
Rockingham is relocated to Kingston; the Rocky Hill moment describes the historical stay without placing the present house at the old location.
The Kingston Mill page questions the Assunpink Trail origin of Princeton-Kingston Road. The overview uses NJDOT’s broader river-road history, not that specific identification.
